summary: Describes how OpenPGP can provide privacy and authentication using the MIME security content types from RFC 1847.

plainLanguage.summary: It shows how to lock and sign email using a well-known lock system.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email with pgp
how does openpgp work with mime email
subtitle: How to wrap OpenPGP signatures and encryption inside MIME email using three content types.

tldr.problem: Earlier ways of mixing PGP with MIME made it impossible to recover a signed message body without parsing PGP-specific data structures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3156 uses the security multiparts of RFC 1847: multipart/signed holds the signed data and a detached OpenPGP signature as separate parts, and multipart/encrypted holds a control part and the encrypted data. It defines the content types application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys.
tldr.outcome: Signed or encrypted OpenPGP email has a defined MIME shape. The RFC updates RFC 2015 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 3156.

facts.label: Parts in encrypted or signed body

today: RFC 3156 is a Proposed Standard from August 2001. It updates RFC 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
Work on combining PGP with MIME before RFC 2015, including the since withdrawn application/pgp content type, suffered from one major problem: you could not recover signed message bodies without parsing PGP-specific data structures. RFC 2015 used the solution from RFC 1847, which defines security multiparts that cleanly separate the signed body from the signature.

RFC 3156 revises RFC 2015 to fit the needs that emerged during the OpenPGP specification work. It defines three content types: application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Old ways of stamping email mixed the stamp into the letter. The new way keeps them in two separate pieces.

sections.title: Data Formats and Transfer Encoding Rules
sections.content:
OpenPGP software can produce ASCII armor or 8-bit binary output. ASCII armor is the REQUIRED method for data transfer, so recipients without the right software can still extract the OpenPGP information. For data too large for one message, the MIME message/partial mechanism SHOULD be used instead of multi-part ASCII armor.

Mail gateways may convert to Quoted-Printable or Base64 when the next hop does not support MIME or 8-bit data, and that would break a signature. So all signed data MUST be limited to 7 bits, with 8-bit data encoded as Quoted-Printable or Base64. This also applies to data that is signed and then encrypted. Implementations MUST also ensure no trailing whitespace remains after MIME encoding.

Lines starting with From should be encoded in Quoted-Printable or Base64, since some mail agents insert a > in front of them and invalidate the signature. Data that is only encrypted may contain 8-bit characters and trailing whitespace. Implementations are advised to accept any content-transfer-encoding but generate only the 7-bit form.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail systems sometimes tidy up a letter in transit. Because tidying would smudge the stamp, the letter must be written in a plain, safe style before it is stamped.

sections.title: Encrypted Messages
sections.content:
Before encryption, data is written in MIME canonical format. An encrypted message uses multipart/encrypted with a protocol parameter of application/pgp-encrypted, and the value MUST be quoted.

The body MUST have exactly two parts. The first has content type application/pgp-encrypted and holds control information, which MUST contain Version: 1. The second holds the encrypted data and MUST be labeled application/octet-stream. The OpenPGP packet format already carries everything else needed to decrypt.
sections.plainLanguage: An encrypted email is a box with two things inside: a small note saying which kind of lock it is, and the locked message itself.

sections.title: Signed Messages
sections.content:
A signed message uses multipart/signed with a protocol parameter of application/pgp-signature (MUST be quoted). The micalg parameter MUST contain exactly one hash symbol of the form pgp-<hash-identifier>, made by lower-casing the hash name and prefixing pgp-. Defined values are pgp-md5, pgp-sha1, pgp-ripemd160, pgp-md2, pgp-tiger192 and pgp-haval-5-160.

The body MUST have exactly two parts: the signed data in MIME canonical form with its content headers, then the OpenPGP signature labeled application/pgp-signature. To sign, the sender converts to canonical form, applies a content-transfer-encoding, adds headers with CRLF line endings, strips trailing whitespace, and calculates the signature over both the data and its content headers. The signature MUST be detached from the signed data.

On receipt, an application MUST convert line endings to canonical CRLF, because a local MTA may have changed them, and pass both the signed data with its headers and the signature to verification.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed email has the letter in one piece and the stamp in another, so you can read the letter without any special tools and still check the stamp.

sections.title: Signing and Encrypting Together
sections.content:
There are two methods. The first, from RFC 1847, signs the data as a multipart/signed body and then encrypts that to form the final multipart/encrypted body. The RFC says this is most useful for standard MIME-compliant forwarding.

The second, the combined method, uses the OpenPGP packet format to sign and encrypt in a single OpenPGP message. It is allowed to reduce processing overhead and increase compatibility with non-MIME OpenPGP implementations. The result is a multipart/encrypted object as in the encrypted case, and it is REQUIRED to follow the same canonicalization rules as multipart/signed. An agent may decrypt a combined message and rewrite it as multipart/signed using the embedded signature.
sections.plainLanguage: You can stamp the letter and then lock it in a box, or use a special lock that stamps and locks in one go.

sections.title: Keys, Security and IANA
sections.content:
Public keys are distributed in a MIME body part with content type application/pgp-keys, which has no required or optional parameters and contains ASCII-armored transferable Public Key Packets.

The only security note specific to this document is that signatures of a canonical text document ignore trailing white space in the signed material, so implementations that use them cannot detect whitespace added in transit. For the underlying protocols, the RFC points to RFC 2046 and RFC 1848.

Under IANA considerations the document registers the three media types. application/pgp-signature uses file extensions asc and sig, and application/pgp-keys uses asc. All three always consist of 7bit text.
sections.plainLanguage: Public keys travel as plain text in their own labeled piece. One small catch is that extra blank spaces added along the way would not be noticed by one kind of stamp.
